paragraphs: Historians who wish to know how many people in early modern Europe could read have long relied on an imperfect proxy: the proportion of people able to sign their names on marriage registers, wills, and legal depositions. The method has obvious attractions. Such documents survive in large numbers, they span every social class, and a signature, unlike a claim to be literate, cannot easily be faked. Yet the proxy rests on an assumption about how reading and writing were taught. In much of early modern Europe, children learned to read first, often at home or in church, and only later—if at all—learned to write, a skill that required paper, ink, and a paid schoolmaster. Many people who could read a catechism or a broadsheet may therefore never have learned to sign their names, so that signature rates probably understate reading ability, perhaps substantially, among the poor and among women, whose schooling was most often cut short.

Ornithologists have proposed that the decline of a migratory songbird in Westmoor Forest is caused by the spread of an invasive shrub, which crowds out the native plants whose berries the birds depend on to refuel during their autumn migration.

Preservationists who seek to protect buildings from the middle of the twentieth century face an obstacle that their predecessors rarely did: much of the public regards the buildings in question as ugly. Campaigns to save Victorian railway stations could appeal to an affection that was already widely felt; campaigns on behalf of concrete civic buildings must first create the affection they hope to mobilize. The most successful of these campaigns have therefore begun not with petitions but with tours, photographs, and exhibitions, efforts to teach the public to see the buildings before asking it to save them.

By the late 1980s, American businesses had been investing heavily in computers for more than a decade, yet measured growth in output per worker had, if anything, slowed. Economists proposed several explanations for this apparent paradox. Some suggested that the benefits of computing were real but poorly captured by statistics designed for an economy of physical goods: faster service and greater product variety, for instance, do not register easily as increased output. Others argued that the investment had simply been too small, relative to the economy as a whole, to make a measurable difference.

A more influential explanation drew on the history of an earlier technology. When electric motors began to replace steam engines in American factories around 1900, productivity gains were negligible for roughly two decades. The reason, economic historians have argued, is that early adopters merely substituted a large electric motor for the central steam engine, leaving intact the system of shafts and belts that the steam engine had required. The decisive gains came only when manufacturers redesigned their plants around small motors attached to individual machines, which allowed single-story layouts organized according to the flow of materials rather than the demands of a central power source. Such redesign required new buildings, new skills, and new methods of management, all of which took time.

By analogy, the slow payoff from computers could be attributed to firms' initial tendency to automate existing procedures rather than to reorganize around the new technology's capabilities. The analogy proved attractive partly because it offered reassurance: it implied that the paradox was temporary, and the acceleration of productivity growth in the late 1990s seemed to bear it out. Yet the analogy's explanatory value is easy to overstate. Because it predicted a lag without specifying how long the lag would last, almost any delay between investment and payoff could be accommodated, and an account that is consistent with nearly every outcome explains less than its proponents may suppose.

Corals that bleach when ocean temperatures rise—expelling the symbiotic algae that supply most of their energy—were long assumed to be doomed unless the heat abated quickly. Some recent observations complicate this picture. Corals on reefs that experience large daily swings in temperature appear to bleach less readily than corals of the same species on more thermally stable reefs, and some corals that survive bleaching reacquire algae of a more heat-tolerant type. Neither finding implies that reefs can withstand indefinite warming; the capacity of corals to adjust may well be outpaced by the rate at which the oceans are heating. But the findings do suggest that the fate of a given reef depends on more than the temperature of the water around it.

Students at Halvorsen High School who attended the school's optional after-school tutoring program last year earned higher average grades than students who did not attend. The principal therefore plans to make the program mandatory for all students next year, expecting that the school's average grades will rise as a result.
